which he might base his confidence and in which he might
find his security, whether the gifts of fate, the achievements
wrought by his own abilities, or the attainments of his
knowledge. In other words, the forgetting of the past means
passing judgment on the old Adam, as it ever emerges out of
the matrix of the past, and especially of the old Adam who
satisfies himself that he is secure.
But there is one thing in his past which Paul does not
forget, namely the experience which shattered his sense of
self-security, which tore him apart from all that he called
his own, bringing a great unrest into his life and yet freeing
him from the fetters of self; one thing he does not forget, the
painful thrust by which Christ gripped his life and cast it
down, and the overwhelming vision of Christ which came to
him in consequence. To this experience he remains faithful;
and thus he remains faithful to that crisis in his past which
liberated him from the dead weight of the past and set him
free to look forward to the boundless horizons of the future.
We are now taking a retrospective survey of that bit of
past time which is closed by the term now ending. We hope
that it may have brought both to those who teach and those
who learn an increase of knowledge and understanding and
an enrichment of life through friendship and fellowship,
through joys of one kind or another, and through deepening
experience and awareness.
What is to be our attitude to all this? Ought we not to
remember it with gratitude? Without a doubt! But the more
we recall these things with sincere gratitude, the more we
shall also become aware that they represent a gift which has
been bestowed on us. And as we say the words: "Lord, I am
too small for all the mercies and all the faithfulness which
Thou hast shown to Thy servant" we shall realize that we are
expressing a judgment on ourselves. Then we shall see in all
